article.overview: A plasma wave instrument measures fluctuations in the electric and/or magnetic field within a plasma, the electrically charged gas that surrounds the Moon in the solar wind. Its sensors pick up waves over a wide frequency range, from very low frequencies up to the megahertz range, and its records show how the plasma is behaving near the spacecraft or the surface. The Moon has no global magnetic field comparable to Earth's (general background; not separately sourced in this rerun), so the solar wind reaches the surface directly and is disturbed by the body itself and by local crustal magnetic anomalies. Plasma waves are therefore a useful diagnostic of those interactions. No dedicated plasma wave instrument on the lunar surface is confirmed as flown in the sources consulted. The lunar record comes mainly from orbiters: the Japanese SELENE (Kaguya) mission carried a wave receiver inside its radar sounder, and the ARTEMIS probes, originally built for Earth magnetosphere work, carried an electric field instrument. A surface instrument, LuSEE-Night, is planned for the far side but had not launched according to the sources consulted.
article.description: A plasma wave instrument consists of one or more sensors that respond to electric or magnetic field changes, a receiver that filters and amplifies the signal, and a digitiser and processor that records the result with a precise time reference. Electric-field sensors are usually long antennas or booms. Magnetic sensors are usually search coils. Electrostatic waves, which are compressive oscillations in the charge density, are detected through their electric field. Electromagnetic waves are detected through both electric and magnetic components. Plasma waves carry information about the local electron density, the temperature and motion of the particles, and the presence of beams or boundaries. For example, a sharp boundary between sunlit plasma and the plasma wake behind the Moon may produce characteristic waves. Measuring these waves is complementary to particle detectors, which count the ions and electrons themselves.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purposes of a lunar plasma wave instrument are: (1) studying the wake behind the Moon, where the Moon blocks the solar wind on its night side; observations of waves at the wake boundary help identify the physical processes that operate there (Hashimoto et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2025). (2) Investigating surface-plasma interaction: electric fields at the dayside surface can be measured and their frequency content compared with models of the plasma sheath above the surface (ARTEMIS EFI observations as summarised in the ARTEMIS literature; LuSEE-Lite measurement goals as described in a NASA slide deck summary). (3) Mapping plasma structure near crustal magnetic anomalies: Kaguya observations reported strong electrostatic solitary waves over localised magnetic anomalies (Hashimoto et al., 2010). (4) Providing context for other lunar measurements: plasma wave data are used with magnetometer and particle data to interpret the plasma environment in which other instruments operate.
article.operating_principle: The sensor couples to the electric or magnetic part of a wave. For electric-field measurements, a pair of antennas or booms is used, and the voltage difference between the sensors is amplified and filtered into frequency bands. Two common modes are sweep-frequency analysis, in which the receiver steps through frequencies and records the signal strength at each step, and waveform capture, in which the signal is digitised and stored for later analysis. The Kaguya Wave-Form Capture (WFC) receiver's WFC-H sub-receiver works in sweep mode covering 1 kHz to 1 MHz, and its WFC-L sub-receiver records waveforms in a lower band (Ono et al., 2010; abstract-level summary). The ARTEMIS Electric Field Instrument (EFI) makes three-axis measurements of the ambient electric field in waveform and spectral modes from DC up to 8 kHz, with a single broadband channel reaching 400 kHz (Bonnell et al., 2008; summary-level source). A companion search coil magnetometer (SCM) supports wave-burst sampling (ARTEMIS literature summaries). Once digitised, the analysis identifies wave modes from frequency, amplitude and polarisation. Electron cyclotron harmonic waves, Langmuir waves and upper hybrid waves have all been reported in lunar plasma observations (Hashimoto et al., 2010, secondary summary).
article.scientific_importance: The Moon is a useful laboratory for plasma physics because it has no thick atmosphere or global magnetosphere. Its surface absorbs particles from the solar wind, and its crustal magnetic anomalies create small magnetic structures that perturb the flow. Plasma wave observations link these local effects with the larger plasma environment. Kaguya observations reported electrostatic solitary waves (ESWs) at three locations: at the wake boundary (Type A), over strong magnetic anomalies (Type B), and in regions where the local magnetic field connects to the lunar surface (Type C, as classified in a secondary summary of Hashimoto et al., 2010). For Type A waves, the original proposal was an electron two-stream instability driven by incoming solar wind electrons and wake electrons accelerated by ambipolar fields at the wake boundary. A 2022 re-examination of an April 2008 event argues that upward electron beams from the nightside surface are an effective source of these waves, which differs from the original interpretation (Nishino et al., 2022, as summarised in a search result; full text not verified). ARTEMIS observations have reported electrostatic shocks inside the lunar wake (Liu et al., 2025), which tests theoretical predictions about wake structure.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a plasma wave instrument. Its design depends on the frequency range, the sensor type, the spacecraft or lander interface, and whether it is an orbiter or surface payload. The examples below are not directly comparable. Where a value is not verified in the sources consulted, it is recorded as null and described as not publicly specified.

examples.name: Kaguya (SELENE) Lunar Radar Sounder - Wave-Form Capture (WFC) receiver
examples.type: Flown lunar orbiter instrument (passive wave receiver within a radar sounder)
examples.status: Flown on Kaguya (SELENE). Instrument paper: Ono et al. (2010).
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources consulted.

frequency_coverage.WFC-H: Fast sweep-frequency analyser, 1 kHz to 1 MHz (Ono et al., 2010; abstract-level summary).
frequency_coverage.WFC-L: Waveform receiver for a lower band; sources disagree on the lower limit (10 Hz in one summary, 100 Hz in another). Not resolved.

examples.antennas: Two orthogonal antennas, reported as 30 m tip-to-tip (Ono et al., 2010; abstract-level summary, not verified against the full paper).
examples.architecture: Software receiver in which most functions are performed by a digital signal processor, with digitised data stored on board.
examples.data_volume: The abstract reports 8,961 hours of natural radio and plasma wave data obtained through 10 June 2009.

examples.name: ARTEMIS Electric Field Instrument (EFI)
examples.type: Flown electric field instrument, developed for THEMIS and re-used at the Moon by the ARTEMIS probes
examples.status: Flown. The EFI was developed for the THEMIS Earth-magnetosphere mission (Bonnell et al., 2008). Two THEMIS probes were placed in lunar orbit as ARTEMIS, which entered lunar orbit in late 2011 according to a secondary source.
examples.sensor_configuration: Three-axis electric field measurements; two pairs of sensors on telescopic booms deployed to 20 m and 25 m, extending perpendicular to the spacecraft's spin cables and along the spin axis (ARTEMIS EFI instrument page).

frequency_coverage.three_axis_waveform_and_spectral: DC to 8 kHz (Bonnell et al., 2008; summary-level source).
frequency_coverage.broadband_channel: Single integral broadband channel to 400 kHz (Bonnell et al., 2008; summary-level source).

examples.companion_sensor: Search coil magnetometer (SCM); wave-burst sampling rates reported in ARTEMIS literature summaries.
examples.development: Sensors built by UC Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory; data processing by University of Colorado LASP; J. Bonnell led the EFI effort.
examples.lunar_observations: High-frequency electrostatic fluctuations of roughly 0.1 to 8 kHz observed over the dayside surface, and electrostatic shocks in the lunar wake (ARTEMIS literature summaries).
examples.caveat: This is an Earth-magnetosphere instrument re-used at the Moon. Its specifications should not be taken as lunar design values.

examples.name: LuSEE-Night (Lunar Surface Electromagnetics Experiment, Night configuration)
examples.type: Planned lunar surface radio spectrometer, primarily a radio astronomy instrument
examples.status: Planned. Project paper describes a developed Concept of Operations. Not launched according to the sources consulted. Launch date unconfirmed; sources disagree (late 2026 in an April 2026 report; 2027 in an aggregator listing that may be a placeholder).
examples.mass_note: Not stated in the arXiv abstract. A secondary source gives a total mass of 128 kg, of which 50 kg is the battery. A 2023 conference paper gives about 40 kg for the battery. These conflict and are not treated as verified.
examples.power_note: The spectrometer must operate through the lunar night on a 7 kWh battery (arXiv:2407.07173), cited as a design constraint for a lunar night of about two weeks. No solar generation figures given.
examples.sensors: Four horizontal monopole antennas forming zenith-pointing beams with two orthogonal linear polarisations (arXiv:2407.07173).
examples.science_goal: Investigate the feasibility of observing the Cosmic Dark Ages through the redshifted 21 cm hydrogen line (arXiv:2407.07173).

examples.name: LuSEE-Lite (earlier related variant)
examples.type: Planned lunar surface electromagnetic sensing package
examples.status: Planned per a NASA slide deck (CP-12, Schrodinger Basin, earlier planned for 2025). Launch status not confirmed in the sources consulted.
examples.measurement_scope: Described in the NASA slide deck as measuring plasma waves, the electric and magnetic field environment from DC to 20 MHz, surface geospacer interactions, lunar surface electrostatic potential and sheath, and dust and electrostatic field interactions.
examples.caveat: Battery and power figures come from a single slide deck and are not verified.

examples.name: Terminator Double Layer Explorer (TerDLE)
examples.status: Proposed. One search result describes a propulsion-driven CubeSat with an ion spectrometer and plasma wave system in elliptical lunar orbit to study the low-altitude wake. Indicated as a concept rather than a funded mission.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No single dimensional envelope applies. The Kaguya WFC is a receiver within a radar sounder whose antennas are reported at 30 m tip-to-tip (abstract-level). ARTEMIS EFI uses booms of 20 m and 25 m. LuSEE-Night uses four horizontal monopole antennas. Dimensions of the electronics enclosures were not verified for any example. Antenna and boom length is driven by the lowest frequency of interest and by the need to isolate the sensors from spacecraft or lander fields.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass values are not publicly specified for the Kaguya WFC receiver or the ARTEMIS EFI in the sources consulted. The LuSEE-Night mass figures conflict between sources (128 kg total with 50 kg battery in one secondary source; about 40 kg battery in a 2023 conference paper) and are not treated as verified. The LuSEE-Lite battery figure (about 43 kg) comes from one slide deck. The examples are not comparable and should not be averaged.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is not publicly specified for the Kaguya WFC or the ARTEMIS EFI in the sources consulted. LuSEE-Night must operate through a lunar night of about two weeks on a 7 kWh battery (arXiv:2407.07173). The LuSEE-Lite power figure of about 15 W comes from a single slide deck and is not verified. A surface instrument's power budget must include thermal survival and heating through the lunar night, which is a general engineering consideration.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The plasma environment around the Moon is shaped by the solar wind, by the wake behind the Moon, and by crustal magnetic anomalies. Dayside surface electrostatic fluctuations at about 0.1 to 8 kHz have been observed by EFI (ARTEMIS literature summaries). A surface plasma wave instrument must also account for the lunar surface electrostatic potential and the sheath above it, which are among the measurement targets listed for LuSEE-Lite (NASA slide deck summary). Surface instruments need a stable power source and thermal control through the lunar night; LuSEE-Night's design, as described in its arXiv abstract, uses a 7 kWh battery for a night of about two weeks. Sensors must be mounted so that structural or lander motion does not contaminate the wave measurements. This is a general engineering consideration and not a sourced requirement for any particular instrument.
article.limitations: A single sensor or small array measures the plasma at one place and time. Separating spatial structure from temporal change needs multiple spacecraft or stations, or a model. Orbital observations from altitudes around 100 km (secondary source for Kaguya) limit direct measurement of the surface sheath. The origin of some observed waves is disputed: the Type A interpretation has been revised in a later study (Nishino et al., 2022). Specifications for some instruments conflict between sources, and some key values (mass, power, Kaguya antenna length) are verified only at abstract level. No flown surface plasma wave instrument is confirmed in the sources consulted.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A plasma wave instrument can be delivered to lunar orbit on an orbiter or to the surface on a lander, depending on its design. The sources consulted describe a planned surface deployment (LuSEE-Night on Firefly's Blue Ghost Mission 2) and past orbital use (Kaguya; ARTEMIS). No deployment has been verified for a dedicated plasma wave payload.
transportation_process: Surface payload (LuSEE-Night, planned): integrate the instrument with the lander on Earth.
Launch the lander on a launch vehicle.
Transfer to the Moon and land on the far side (Nassau Crater, per the Firefly mission page as seen in a search result; not fetched).
Deploy the instrument on the lander's top deck and connect power and data.

Operate through the lunar day; the lander is designed to shut down before lunar night so it does not interfere with the instrument, and the instrument survives the night on its battery (Firefly mission page summary; battery per arXiv:2407.07173).
Orbiter payloads (Kaguya WFC; ARTEMIS EFI): integrate with the spacecraft, launch, transfer, orbit insertion, boom deployment and commissioning. Individual steps were not verified for these missions.
Proposed CubeSat (TerDLE): requires a delivery route to lunar orbit and propulsion for an elliptical orbit. No compatibility assessment possible from the sources consulted.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Electric-field instruments use telescopic booms or long antennas. ARTEMIS EFI booms were deployed to 20 m and 25 m. LuSEE-Night uses four horizontal monopole antennas. Kaguya's antennas are reported at 30 m tip-to-tip (abstract-level). Surface deployment method for LuSEE-Night was not verified in the sources consulted.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Kaguya (SELENE) carried the LRS Wave-Form Capture receiver in lunar orbit. ARTEMIS re-used THEMIS-built EFI and SCM sensors in lunar orbit after 2011 (secondary source). No historical surface plasma wave instrument is confirmed in the sources consulted.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility of any plasma wave payload with a named lander or spacecraft has not been verified. It would need comparison of mass, dimensions, mounting, boom or antenna clearances, landing or orbit loads, power, thermal and data interfaces against verified spacecraft documentation. No compatibility claim is made in this article.

article.historical_significance: Kaguya's Lunar Radar Sounder and its Wave-Form Capture receiver produced an extended record of natural radio and plasma waves around the Moon, reported in Ono et al. (2010) and later plasma wave studies. Hashimoto et al. (2010) reported electrostatic solitary waves at the wake boundary and over magnetic anomalies, a key early result. ARTEMIS observations of electrostatic shocks in the wake (Liu et al., 2025) extend this work. LuSEE-Night, if launched, would provide a surface radio and electromagnetic environment measurement on the far side.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Mass, power and dimensions are not publicly specified for the Kaguya WFC receiver or the ARTEMIS EFI in the sources consulted. LuSEE-Night mass figures conflict across sources, and LuSEE-Lite battery and power figures rest on one slide deck. The Kaguya WFC-L lower frequency limit differs between sources (10 Hz or 100 Hz). The Nishino et al. (2022) full text, the Liu et al. (2025) PDF and the Ono et al. (2010) and Bonnell et al. (2008) full texts were not retrieved; their values are abstract-level or summary-level. The Springer pages for Bonnell et al. (2008) and the Earth, Planets and Space article redirected to a sign-in page and were not followed. LuSEE-Night launch status and date were not confirmed from an official source. The TerDLE concept is described only in one search result. Lander compatibility has not been verified against interface documents.
